title: LLM: Spiral to Turing Machine
category_reason: Frames LLM internals (residual stream + attention) as a topological spiral that, sliced, becomes a discrete Turing machine — an interpretability story about how an LLM computes.
thesis: An LLM's layered computation is a high-dimensional residual stream drawn as a spiral that the attention plane 'slices' into a 1-D binary tape, so the network's per-layer processing can be read as a Turing machine in states like SEARCHING_OPEN_BRACKET / FOUND_PATTERN_MATCH.
key_claims: The high-dimensional residual stream is a spiral in hidden-state space; 'slicing' it at a specific angle 'collapses the complex geometry into discrete bits'.
The attention plane is the 'algorithm filter': where the spiral crosses the plane (|plane_y - (i-4)| < 0.3) the corresponding tape cell flips to 1, else 0.
Mechanistic loop: (1) Read — attention head scans the slice; (2) Match — if bit is 1 update the internal vector; (3) Write — move to next layer = next turn of the spiral.
The machine has discrete states shown live (SEARCHING_OPEN_BRACKET, FOUND_PATTERN_MATCH, SCANNING_EMBEDDINGS), i.e. LLM layer-stacking is framed as a state machine.
Only the 1-D intersections (bits) are 'the discrete bits extracted by the model to perform algorithmic logic'; the 3-D spiral itself is latent/hidden.
methods_math: residual stream as a space curve (Catmull-Rom / TubeGeometry spiral)
visualizations: three.js 3-D scene: blue spiral tube (CatmullRom + TubeGeometry) intersecting a moving white 'attention' plane (rAF, plane y = sin(t)*4, spiral spins)
DOM side panel: 8-cell binary tape that flips 0/1 as the plane passes, plus a live Turing-state readout
internal_tensions: The 1/0 'hit' rule (|plane_y - (i-4)| < 0.3) is an aesthetic threshold, not a real attention computation — the claim that attention 'extracts discrete bits' is asserted, not derived.
Presents LLMs as Turing machines via analogy, but no actual weights/QKV/softmax are shown; the 'Turing' framing is interpretive, not proven.
Conflates the continuous residual stream with a discrete tape; the discretization is the whole claim and is unargued.

title: Prime Latent Manifold
category_reason: Number-theory visualization of prime gaps dressed in ML vocabulary ('latent manifold', 'feature space'); there is no neural net or learned model, so no real AI application.
thesis: A canvas demo that projects the 'rhythm' of consecutive prime gaps (four primes at a time, log of their gaps) into a 2-D 'latent space' so the reader can look for 'ghost structures' — clusters that would not exist if primes were truly random.
key_claims: The feature vector for each window is the set of gaps (p_{n+1}-p_n, p_{n+2}-p_{n+1}, p_{n+3}-p_{n+2}); these are the 'local geometry of randomness'.
Coordinates are x_lat = log(g1)cos(rot) - log(g2)sin(rot), y_lat = log(g2)cos(rot+warp) + log(g3)sin(rot+warp) — a rotation of log-gap features, then warped by tan(warp*0.1).
The 4th gap g4 (the 'future' of the sequence) is used only for coloring, implying a 'prediction' axis the eye is invited to read.
Explicit task: 'Search for Ghost Structures — clusters that shouldn't exist if primes were truly random.'
Primes are generated by a sieve of Eratosthenes up to 1,500,000 (Uint8Array); the visible count is a slider from 1000 to 80000.
visualizations: canvas 2-D scatter: each prime window a 1-px dot, hue from the 4th gap (g4*10), additive 'lighter' blending for density; four sliders (N, Warp lambda, Dimensional Rotation, Topological Zoom) drive a re-render
internal_tensions: Invites the reader to 'find' non-random clusters, but the projection is a fixed, arbitrary map of log-gaps — it can only re-project known primes, not discover genuine structure; any 'ghost' is an artifact of the chosen transform.
Uses 'latent manifold' / 'feature space' as metaphor while doing no embedding learning or distance metric, so the ML framing is decorative.
The 4th gap is 'the future' but only used for color, so the apparent prediction is not tested.

title: LLM Topological Spiral Visualization
category_reason: Interpretability visualization of an LLM's residual stream as a spiral sliced by the attention plane into discrete bits — an argument about what the model computes.
thesis: The residual stream evolving through an LLM's layers is a spiral in high-dimensional space; the attention 'slice' (a plane) only captures the 1-D intersections (red dots), and those intersections are the discrete bits the model uses for algorithmic logic.
key_claims: The spiral is 'the residual stream evolving through layers' (hidden-state journey).
The white plane is 'the Attention Slice' and 'only captures 1D intersections (the red dots) of the higher-dimensional spiral'.
The red dots are 'the discrete bits (0/1) extracted by the model to perform algorithmic logic'.
Bits are conceptual approximations placed on the plane and pulsate (scale 1/0) to represent a 0/1 state — i.e. on/off attention activity.
The plane moves up and down (sin) to simulate 'different slices' as the head's context window changes.
methods_math: residual stream as a growing spiral (Catmull-Rom / TubeGeometry)
visualizations: three.js 3-D scene: blue spiral tube (radius grows with t) + moving white slice plane + 5 red bit-spheres that track the plane and pulse 0/1 (rAF; plane y = sin(t)*3, spiral spins)
three overlay labels explaining spiral = residual stream, plane = attention slice, red dots = discrete bits
internal_tensions: The bit placement is explicitly a 'conceptual approximation for the visual' — the code admits the 0/1 dots do not come from a real attention computation.
Asserts attention 'extracts discrete bits' but shows no softmax/QKV; the discretization is aesthetic, not mechanistic.
The spiral's radius grows linearly with layer index, a visual choice with no stated model justification.

title: Prime Harmonic Interference (Harmonic Sieve)
category_reason: Number-theory visualization placing primes by their remainder modulo m to reveal modular 'resonance'; no ML model, so no AI application despite the physics-flavored 'harmonic' language.
thesis: A 'harmonic sieve': primes are plotted at x = (p mod m)/m and y = p/LIMIT, so that when the modulus slider lands on an integer (e.g. 30, 42, 60) the primes align into vertical 'columns of truth', visualized as 'Harmonic Resonance' of prime gaps.
key_claims: Each prime p is positioned by its remainder: x = (p % m)/m * width, y = (p/LIMIT)*height, with m a continuous 'Harmonic Modulus (Frequency)' slider (2..100).
'When you hit an integer (like 30, 42, 60), the primes will align into perfect vertical columns of truth' — i.e. modular alignment is the exhibited phenomenon.
Color (hue) is the remainder scaled around the color wheel (remainder*(360/m) + offset), so each residue class gets a distinct hue; primes divisible by 100 get a glow.
The mouse hover reports a 'MODULO PHASE' and claims 'any alignment here indicates a Constellation of primes separated by multiples of the modulus'.
Primes come from a sieve up to LIMIT = 50,000.
methods_math: modular arithmetic / residue classes (p mod m)
harmonic/wave 'resonance' as a metaphor for modular alignment
visualizations: canvas 2-D prime 'beam' plot: each prime a 2x4 rect at (mod-m position, p/LIMIT), hue by residue, glow every 100th; three sliders (Modulus, Visual Density, Chroma Offset) + a hover 'SCANNING LINE' inspector reporting the modulo phase
internal_tensions: The 'Harmonic Resonance' / 'columns of truth' language is dramatic, but modular alignment (primes of a fixed residue stacking vertically) is a trivial consequence of p mod m being constant — there is no deep 'harmonic' structure being shown.
A continuous modulus m makes 'p % m' use the floored integer, so the 'resonance' is really integer-mod behavior; the smooth slider is somewhat misleading about what changes.
The hover text asserts a 'Constellation' of primes separated by multiples of the modulus without quantifying or testing it.

title: Projektions-Demonstrator: Punkt-zu-Linie (Klarheit durch Farb-Projektion)
category_reason: Pure geometry demo of central (perspective) projection of 2-D points onto a 1-D line; no AI/ML model or application, just projective geometry and dimensionality reduction.
thesis: A color-coded central-projection demonstrator: four colored 2-D points are projected from a movable light source onto a 1-D 'wall', and the colors let you trace exactly which point in 2-D lands at which position on the 1-D line.
key_claims: 'Jeder farbige Punkt im Raum wird auf die 1D-Wand projiziert' — every colored point in the space is projected onto the 1-D wall.
'Durch die Farben siehst du genau, welcher Punkt im 2D-Raum welche Position auf der 1D-Linie einnimmt' — the colors are the device that makes the 2-D -> 1-D mapping legible.

Projection is central/perspective from a light source fixed on the left X-rail: the ray from light through point P meets the wall at shadowY = light.y + (p.y - light.y)*t, with t = (wallX - light.x)/(p.x - light.x).
The light source is driven by mouse Y (moving along the vertical rail), and each projection changes the landing positions on the wall.
Four labeled points A (red), B (green), C (blue), D (magenta) are the fixed 2-D objects; their wall images are labeled A', B', C', D'.
methods_math: central / perspective projection (light source -> point -> screen ray)
projective ray intersection, t = (wallX - light.x)/(p.x - light.x)
linear interpolation along the projection ray
visualizations: canvas 2-D: four colored source points, transparent colored projection rays to a vertical 1-D wall, glowing projected dots (A'..D'), and a mouse-driven yellow light source constrained to a left rail
internal_tensions: It is a clean 2-D -> 1-D projection, but the demo has no notion of information loss, overlap, or reconstruction — the hard part of real dimensionality reduction (which points collide, is the map invertible?) is left implicit.

Projection from a single 1-D-moving light source cannot separate all four points in general; collisions are possible but not surfaced, so 'Klarheit' (clarity) holds only for this particular configuration.
